clue.text: Not left by those who go hand-in-glove

definitions.text: Not left by those who go hand-in-glove

parts.words: Not left by those who go hand-in-glove
parts.note: a gloved hand leaves no marks from its fingertips, so burglars who wear gloves leave none behind; 'hand-in-glove' usually means in close league

explanation.surface: Something that close partners in crime never leave behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand-in-glove' normally means working closely together; read literally, it is a hand inside a glove, which leaves no marks.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloved criminals avoid leaving the tell-tale skin-ridge marks police use to identify suspects.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: the clue is wordplay alone, as early Times puzzles sometimes allowed, and the crossings settle the word

indicators.note: an extract is a piece taken out of a text, so the letters lie inside the book title

parts.note: the word in the book title whose letters hold the answer

explanation.surface: A quotation from A. S. M. Hutchinson's popular 1921 novel If Winter Comes.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters sit inside 'Winter'; the clue offers no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury; the clue gives no synonym, only the title the letters lie in.

clue.text: How to speed up the crop in Kongwa

definitions.note: No real definition is printed: the clue is wordplay alone, as early Times puzzles sometimes allowed, and these link words stand where one would be

parts.note: to ginger up is to liven or hurry along
Kongwa in Tanganyika was the centre of the British groundnut (peanut) scheme of the late 1940s

explanation.surface: Advice on hurrying the harvest of the troubled Tanganyika groundnut scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kongwa groundnut scheme was a costly 1940s British failure, much in the news in 1950.
explanation.definitionFit: These are crisp biscuits flavoured with the spice root; the clue gives only the two pieces.

definitions.note: the whole clue reads the word as a fresh pairing; it means mends

parts.note: again signals the prefix meaning once more, set in front
matching two things is putting them in pairs

explanation.surface: A question about matching a couple up once more.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads the word as pairing up afresh, a pun on its everyday sense of mends.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means mends or fixes, but the clue reads it as matching couples once more.

parts.note: chez is French for at the home of; Lady Catherine de Bourgh is the haughty aristocrat of Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, so this asks for the name of her Kent estate

explanation.walkthrough: The OCR text reads 'Bough'; the page prints 'Bourgh'. The answer is Rosings Park, the estate Elizabeth Bennet visits in Kent.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Catherine's grand house in Kent, where Mr Collins is her rector, bears this name in Austen's novel.

parts.note: Shakespeare's winter song in Love's Labour's Lost has Dick the shepherd blowing on his fingertip to warm it

explanation.surface: A country shepherd playing something, perhaps a pipe or horn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When icicles hang by the wall, And Dick the shepherd blows his nail', from the closing song of Love's Labour's Lost.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song, a cold shepherd warms his fingertip by breathing on it.

parts.note: Latin sine means without, so the word split in two would describe ailments with no remedy; its real sense is undemanding posts

explanation.surface: A question whether lasting ailments are beyond treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: Split after its fourth letter, the word reads as Latin 'without' plus remedies; chronic illnesses have none.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means paid posts that require little or no work, originally church offices without care of souls.

clue.text: They don't seem to look where they're going

definitions.text: They don't seem to look where they're going

parts.words: They don't seem to look where they're going
parts.note: people who walk while still asleep move about with eyes unseeing, apparently heedless of their path

explanation.surface: A grumble about careless pedestrians.
explanation.walkthrough: It sounds like careless walkers, but these people are actually asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Somnambulists move about in their sleep, eyes open but not taking in their route.

indicators.note: change tells us the letters of won't a are to be rearranged

parts.note: the letters W, O, N, T and A, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A question whether a deity refuses to alter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' is the anagram signal working on WONTA.
explanation.definitionFit: Wotan is the German name for Odin, chief of the Norse gods, as in Wagner's Ring cycle.

clue.text: Not to be confused with the man who takes the gate-money

definitions.text: Not to be confused with the man who takes the gate-money

parts.words: Not to be confused with the man who takes the gate-money
parts.note: a wicket is also a small gate, so a cricket fielder's title could be mistaken for a gatekeeper's

explanation.surface: A warning not to mix someone up with the turnstile attendant at a match.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR text adds 'if'; the page has none. A wicket is also a gate, and in cricket the fielder behind the stumps has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: The cricket fielder who stands behind the batsman's stumps, not someone collecting entrance money.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the abbreviation anag. is the setter's open instruction to rearrange the letters of the words before it

parts.note: the letters of all three words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A sigh at being denied even a sip of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: In 1950 a clue could be a bare anagram with no definition; the crossing letters confirm the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Passional means relating to strong emotion, and also names a book of saints' sufferings.

clue.text: These might appropriately have been her jewels, who, showed her children

definitions.text: These might appropriately have been her jewels, who, showed her children

parts.words: These might appropriately have been her jewels, who, showed her children
parts.note: Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, famously presented her sons as her jewels; red gemstones sharing her name would suit her

explanation.surface: A Roman matron's famous answer about her treasures, given a gemstone twist.
explanation.walkthrough: Asked to show her jewels, the Roman matron Cornelia pointed to her children; the stones named after her would have been fitting ones.
explanation.definitionFit: These reddish semi-precious stones, also spelt carnelians, carry a name echoing Cornelia herself.

indicators.note: the letter A of came is sent to the top, the front of the word, ahead of the C

explanation.surface: Someone rose to the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: moving the A of 'Came' 'to the top' builds the word, and reaching the summit is what it means.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the peak or highest point, so arriving there is coming to the summit.

clue.text: Reasonable profit from the swings and roundabouts ?

definitions.meaning: a just and decent yield on an investment
swings and roundabouts are rides at a funfair, so coming back from them is coming home from a fair

explanation.surface: A businessman hoping that gains and losses even out to a decent profit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swings and roundabouts' suggests things evening out, but here they are literal funfair rides.
explanation.definitionFit: A just yield on money invested; also, the trip back home from a funfair.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: the clue is wordplay alone, as early Times puzzles sometimes allowed, and the crossings settle the word

indicators.note: the scrambled peace goes between letters of ends, splitting that word in two

parts.note: the word ends itself

indicators.note: broken signals that the letters of the Latin word for peace are jumbled

parts.note: pax is the Latin word for peace

explanation.surface: A shattered truce separates the extremities.
explanation.walkthrough: The peace is Latin, not English. There is no real definition: early Times puzzles sometimes printed wordplay alone and let the crossings settle the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means grows larger or spreads out; the clue itself offers no synonym for it.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: early Times anagram clues gave only the letters to rearrange, and this marker stands where a definition would be

indicators.note: the abbreviation anag. is the setter's open instruction to rearrange the letters of the words before it

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A slip-up by someone from Cuba.
explanation.walkthrough: A bare anagram with no definition, as 1950 Times puzzles sometimes printed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means innkeepers, or tax collectors in the Roman world of the Gospels.

definitions.note: No definition is printed: the clue is wordplay alone, as early Times puzzles sometimes allowed, and this link word stands where one would be

parts.note: to spar is to box in practice
to row is to pull on the oars

explanation.surface: A sporting schedule: boxing followed by rowing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives only the two pieces, with no definition of the small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a small brown bird common around houses and gardens; the clue offers no synonym.

clue.text: Short of khaki? Fold it round a bit for a tent

indicators.note: the folded word goes around a bit, holding it in its middle
folding the shortened word in the middle brings its back half to the front
khaki is cut short by losing one of its letters, its H

parts.note: the word khaki itself
a bit is simply the word bit

explanation.surface: A puzzle about folding khaki canvas round something to pitch a shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of' drops the H, leaving KAKI; 'Fold' swaps its halves to KIKA, which goes 'round' the bit. The surface's question mark asks you to read khaki as letters, not cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A kibitka is a Russian covered wagon or the felt tent of Central Asian nomads.

parts.note: a single plain definition: a malady is an illness

explanation.walkthrough: A one-word plain definition with no wordplay, as early puzzles sometimes printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean an illness or disorder, usually a minor or chronic one.

clue.text: It has a place in the sun

definitions.text: It has a place in the sun

parts.words: It has a place in the sun
parts.note: a place in the sun usually means a favourable position; literally, a sunshade is put up out in strong sunlight

explanation.surface: Something that has found a comfortable, favoured spot in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A place in the sun' is an idiom for good fortune; read literally, it is where a sunshade is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A light umbrella carried or set up to give shade from strong sunshine.

parts.note: an executioner selecting his beheading blade would be choosing his chopper; split, the word says just that

explanation.surface: A question whether the executioner gets to select something.
explanation.walkthrough: Split after its fourth letter, the word reads as choosing a chopper, which a headsman might do.
explanation.definitionFit: A digging tool with a pointed iron head, which the clue reads as selecting a chopper.

indicators.note: being engaged in the word sericulture means sitting inside its letters

explanation.surface: A man who works at silkworm farming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is engaged in' says the name sits inside 'sericulture', the rearing of silkworms.
explanation.definitionFit: Eric is a man's name, so 'He' stands for any man so called.

clue.text: Dearth in a small hound is an order

indicators.note: the word for dearth goes inside the name of the hound

parts.note: a beagle is a small hound used for hunting hares
a dearth is a lack

explanation.surface: A shortage within a little dog is declared to be a decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the shortage after the first letter of the hound. The definition means an order of knighthood, not a command.
explanation.definitionFit: The Order of the Black Eagle was the highest order of chivalry of the Kingdom of Prussia.

indicators.note: read as 'made of': the definition is formed out of the letters of a girl, rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.surface: How big a young woman is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'size' is not dimensions but a glaze or sealing coat. Only the slight 'of' signals that 'a girl' is to be rearranged, a looseness 1950 setters allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: Size is a gluey wash used as a sealant; egg-white glaze serves the same purpose for bookbinders.

clue.text: Found in the early stages of progressive tuition

definitions.note: No real definition is printed: these words point to the start of tuition, where the letters end, and stand where a definition would be

indicators.note: being found in the words means the letters lie inside them, spanning both

explanation.surface: Something met with in the first lessons of a graded course.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'progressive' into 'tuition'. 'The early stages' points to the start of 'tuition'.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles or cosmetics; the clue gives no synonym.

clue.text: He keeps William from the bag

definitions.text: He keeps William from the bag

parts.words: He keeps William from the bag
parts.note: the Victorian prime minister William, Gladstone was named with a middle name between his first name and his surname, which is also a kind of bag

explanation.surface: Someone stops a man called William getting at a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: A Gladstone bag is a hinged travelling bag named after the prime minister; his middle name stands between 'William' and 'Gladstone'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Gladstone's full name had this middle name, which sits between his first name and surname.

parts.note: Harriet Beecher Stowe wrote Uncle Tom's Cabin

explanation.walkthrough: A plain general-knowledge definition: Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel Uncle Tom's Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Eva is the saintly girl in Uncle Tom's Cabin, the novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe.

indicators.note: read as 'made of': the definition is formed out of the letters of a slur, rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words, taken as written

explanation.surface: How far an insult can carry.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the slight 'of' signals that 'a slur' is to be rearranged, a looseness 1950 setters allowed; 'Range' may also hint at arranging.
explanation.definitionFit: The Urals are the mountain chain dividing European Russia from Siberia.

parts.note: a patron saint is the protector of a group; the breed of big Alpine rescue dogs is named after the hospice of this saint

explanation.walkthrough: The saint founded the Alpine hospice whose monks bred the famous rescue dogs, which carry his name.
explanation.definitionFit: The great rescue dog breed is named after the saint whose hospice in the Alps bred them.
